extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, dramatists, and educated readers of Romantic-era dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for judging and composing dramatic works (plot, character, moral purpose, probability, stagecraft) as discussed in a Romantic-era literary-criticism essay. Useful for critics and playwrights assessing taste and dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid zoological rarities and stage barbarisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The British stage should be redeemed "not only from horses, dog's, elephants, and the like zoological rarities, but also from the more pernicious barbarisms and Kotzebuesm in morals and taste."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle for spectacle's sake (imported 'speaking monsters' or exotic animals) and theatrical barbarisms corrupt taste; a reformed stage should emphasize classical renown and moral/tasteful presentation rather than sensational zoological attractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of responsible theatre management
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers/trustees entrusted with reform should possess "Rank, fortune, liberal education, and (their natural accompaniments, or consequences) critical discernment, delicate tact, disinterestedness, unsuspected morals, notorious patriotism, and tried Mæcenas-ship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mercenary manager whose 'lucri bonus odor' dominates will corrupt theatrical reform; management should be guided by disinterestedness, education, and patriotic/ethical motives to restore good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lessing's dramatic virtues and defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing's dramas are said to have a "deficiency ... in depth and imagination: their excellence is in the construction of the plot; the good sense of the sentiments; the sobriety of the morals; and the high polish of the diction and dialogue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramas for both imaginative depth and technical virtues: strong plot construction, sensible sentiment, moral sobriety, and polished diction/dialogue are commendable even where imaginative depth may be lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance generic (representative) and individual (definite) for ideal characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ideal consists in the happy balance of the generic with the individual." An ideal/heroic character combines the representative (symbolic) and the definite (individual) elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be simultaneously representative (instructive/applicable to classes) and individual (definite, specific) — excess of either element (mere abstraction or mere portrait) spoils the ideal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability depends on internal harmony, not literal likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: A "dramatic probability" sufficient for pleasure may exist "even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility." The poet asks only that the reader yield to a dream: "the poet does not require us to be awake and believe; he solicits us only to yield ourselves to a dream."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improbable or supernatural incidents are acceptable provided the whole work is in harmony, internally consistent, and sustains the requisite imaginative 'negative faith' from the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supernatural permitted if consistent with overall effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes such as the ghost-interventions in Don Juan are defensible: the audience need not 'believe' literally but must accept the dream-state; the "very extravagance of the incidents... prevents the wickedness from shocking our minds."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural elements must be integrated coherently into the drama's imaginative logic so they enhance rather than break the audience's willing suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray intellectual power alongside moral conflict to heighten interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The "co-existence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest"; such heterogenous coordination lets us contemplate intellect as self-subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic interest is increased when a character's great intellect or power is juxtaposed with culpability or moral failure; this tension reveals character and engages the audience deeply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making wickedness the subject of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted margin note: "Wickedness is no subject for Comedy. This was Congreve's great error..." and further: "The absence of Virtue is no deficiency... Wickedness [is] a great defect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should not center on wickedness or treat vice as the primary subject; moral interest and some virtuous engagement are required for enduring comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Gothic/sensational tropes when used as mere poetical amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of romantic sensationalism: "the ruined castles, the dungeons, the trap-doors, the skeletons, the flesh-and-blood ghosts, and the perpetual moonshine... when [the author] makes sin, death, and sorrow a poetical amusement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gothic or horrific devices risk becoming superficial ornamentation if they are employed only to produce impressive writing; they should arise from genuine imaginative necessity or moral/poetic purpose, not as affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama should expose the hollowness of external accomplishments when detached from virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Alheïsta Fulminata (Don Juan-type drama) "presents an exquisite portraiture" of gentlemanly accomplishments "for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness, and in order to put us on our guard by demonstrating their utter indifference to vice and virtue, whenever these... are contemplated for themselves alone."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate moral purpose of drama can be to show that external qualities (honor, courage, refined feeling) are hollow without principled virtue — i.e., use display to instruct morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding criminals by confusing natural causes and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'modern Jacobinical drama' succeeds by "the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things in their causes and effects," exciting surprise by representing liberal qualities in classes where experience teaches us least to expect them, and "rewarding... criminals" with sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic design should preserve a plausible moral/causal order rather than manufacture sympathy for criminality through contrived surprise; false moral equivalences undermine the drama's ethical coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize criminal characters with wit, gaiety, and refined manners to maintain complex interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The "constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity, which prevents the criminal, even in his most atrocious moments, from sinking into the mere ruffian... the fine suffusion... of the characteristic manners and feelings, of a highly-bred gentleman, gives life to the drama."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraying social graces, wit, and gentlemanly manners in an otherwise criminal character preserves dramatic complexity and audience interest; these traits should be balanced so the character remains morally instructive rather than glamourized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal/formal definition of ideal art (species through individual form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin formulations offered: e.g. "Forma formans per formam formatam translucens" and a fuller rendering: "Species specificata per formam individualizatam sive Individuum etc..." — the idea that the species (form) is expressed through a determined individual form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic instructs that ideal poetic art is achieved when universal (species) qualities are manifested through a fully determinate individual instance; practitioners should aim to realize universal truths within individual characters/figures.
